title: Diversity and the right to education: The evolution of inclusion in Spanish law (1970–2020)
text_snippet: Diversity and the right to education: The evolution of inclusion in Spanish law (1970–2020) Abstract This article analyses the evolution of attention to diversity and inclusion in the Spanish education system through a critical study of organic education laws from 1970 to the present. Using a qualitative‐descriptive and interpretative approach, it examines the conceptualisation and terminology used, the underlying theoretical models and the schooling measures proposed in each regulation. The results show the coexistence of different models—medical‐rehabilitative, social, biopsychosocial, human rights, among others—which have shaped an unstable legislative framework with significant tensions between integration and inclusion. Although since the 1990s, laws have explicitly incorporated the discourse of inclusion, terminological, structural and practical contradictions persist, hindering its consolidation in schools. It is concluded that the absence of a common model of inclusion, together with legislative instability and regional decentralisation, generates partial advances but also setbacks, highlighting the need for in‐depth and qualitative assessments to ensure truly inclusive education.

title: Neurodivergent pupils' school distress and attendance difficulties: Staff insights and experiences
text_snippet: Neurodivergent pupils' school distress and attendance difficulties: Staff insights and experiences Abstract Increasing numbers of children and young people (CYP) are experiencing attendance difficulties in the UK. A crucial underpinning reason for the increase is school distress, where CYP experience such high levels of distress and anxiety that they cannot attend. Evidence suggests that neurodivergent CYP disproportionately experience school distress and attendance difficulties. Previous research has predominantly focused on insights from parents and sometimes CYP. Insights from staff working with neurodivergent CYP experiencing school distress and attendance difficulties are relatively lacking. Therefore, online semi‐structured interviews were conducted with 16 members of school staff. Three themes were constructed via reflexive thematic analysis: (1) A complex picture of needs and challenges ; (2) Staff are only human ; and (3) An education system where nobody is thriving . The findings highlighted that the school environment was challenging for neurodivergent pupils. Furthermore, staff could not sufficiently support CYP within the under‐resourced education system and called for a more inclusive/sustainable system. title: Differentiated instruction for gifted students and their peers in a Swedish year 1 primary school classroom: A focused ethnographic mixed‐methods study
text_snippet: Differentiated instruction for gifted students and their peers in a Swedish year 1 primary school classroom: A focused ethnographic mixed‐methods study Abstract This study explores how differentiated instruction (DI) is planned, implemented and evaluated in a Swedish Year 1 classroom that includes two gifted students. Applying a focused ethnographic mixed‐methods design, it combines qualitative data with structured observations using the Classroom Observation Scales‐Revised (COS‐R). Thematic analysis was structured around three themes: planning for DI involving anticipation and collaboration (e.g. adjusting to students' readiness), implementing DI through a responsive and flexible practices (e.g. real‐time adaptations), and evaluating DI through ongoing reflection (e.g. formative assessment in classroom interactions). This supported both academic growth and social inclusion. COS‐R scores indicated strengths in curriculum planning ( M = 2.50) and creative thinking ( M = 2.50), and areas for improvement in critical thinking ( M = 1.50) and research strategies ( M = 1.13). The study shows how DI can be integrated into everyday classroom practice in ways that respond to student diversity. title: Reorganising the conditions of participation: Effects of differentiated instruction on the social dimension of inclusive education
text_snippet: Reorganising the conditions of participation: Effects of differentiated instruction on the social dimension of inclusive education Abstract This study examines the effectiveness of a structured Differentiated Instruction (DI) programme, implemented as a universal practice for learning “Differentiation for All”, in enhancing the social dimension of inclusive education for students with mild intellectual disabilities in second and third‐grade inclusive primary classrooms. A mixed‐methods approach was adopted, using a pre–post design with an intervention and a comparison group. The study included 32 students with mild intellectual disabilities, 202 typically developing peers, and 30 general‐education teachers. Data were collected through systematic observations, sociometric techniques, and semi‐structured interviews. Quantitative findings showed that after the intervention, the intervention group demonstrated a statistically significant increase in social interaction with typically developing peers and an improvement in social acceptance, whereas the comparison group showed no comparable changes. Qualitative data indicated a trend toward increased perceived peer support, particularly in terms of invitations to participate, positive attention, and greater participation in school activities. title: Distinct or similar? Career choice motivation in preservice special education and secondary school teachers

Career choice motivation in preservice special education and secondary school teachers Abstract Career choice motives play a central role in teacher development, professional commitment and retention. Although special education is often assumed to attract individuals with strong pedagogical and altruistic motives and lower extrinsic orientations, empirical evidence is inconsistent. This study examines whether preservice special education teachers in Germany differ systematically in their career choice motives from preservice secondary school teachers. Data were drawn from two samples in Baden‐Württemberg, Germany: 703 preservice special education teachers and 1012 preservice secondary school teachers. Career choice motives were assessed using self‐reports. After establishing the factorial validity and partial scalar invariance, latent mean analyses were conducted controlling for age and gender. title: When inclusion meets the curriculum: How students with and without SEN in Croatia see their teachers' inclusive practices
text_snippet: When inclusion meets the curriculum: How students with and without SEN in Croatia see their teachers' inclusive practices Abstract This study examines lower secondary students' perceptions of inclusive teaching practices in Croatia, with a focus on personalisation and differentiation. It also evaluates the psychometric properties and measurement invariance of the Croatian version of the Inclusive Teaching Practices Scale—Students' version (ITPS‐S). The sample comprised 1317 sixth‐ and seventh‐grade students, including students with and without special educational needs (SEN). Confirmatory factor analysis supported the expected two‐factor structure of the ITPS‐S, and the scale demonstrated strong reliability and full measurement invariance across SEN status, gender, grade level and partial invariance across subject domain (Croatian language & Mathematics). Overall, students reported moderate use of inclusive practices, indicating that personalisation and differentiation are present but not yet implemented intensively. No differences were found between students with SEN and their peers or between genders. However, younger students perceived higher levels of inclusive practices than older students. title: Exploring neuro‐inclusivity by design in assessment: A scoping review
text_snippet: Exploring neuro‐inclusivity by design in assessment: A scoping review Abstract Understanding of neurodivergent characteristics remains limited in educational assessment, which hinders inclusive design approaches. Consequently, assessment design processes can fail to prevent unintended barriers being introduced in assessment, which can negatively impact neurodivergent learners' academic performance and emotional wellbeing. Guided by PRISMA‐ScR guidelines, a scoping review was conducted to examine neurodivergent learners' assessment challenges and neuro‐inclusive assessment design strategies. Overall, 23 studies were reviewed. Autism, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and dyslexia were most frequently examined in the literature, with neurodevelopmental differences such as dyspraxia and dyscalculia underrepresented. Following a grounded theory approach to qualitative data analysis, three broad themes emerged from the review: (1) pedagogical considerations, (2) understanding neurodivergent learners and (3) approaches to assessment. Pedagogical considerations include a need for greater awareness amongst educators and improved institutional infrastructures to foster inclusive learning environments. title: Autistic Children's self‐reported social satisfaction: Comparison with observer‐ and teacher‐reported perspectives
text_snippet: Autistic Children's self‐reported social satisfaction: Comparison with observer‐ and teacher‐reported perspectives Abstract We conducted a small‐scale exploratory study of how autistic children report on their loneliness and social (dis)satisfaction in the classroom, and whether child self‐reports related to teacher‐reported peer social integration or observed positive peer interactions. Child participants ( n = 18) were in kindergarten through second grade, identified by their teachers ( n = 18) as either having been diagnosed with or demonstrating the characteristics of autism. At three time points over roughly 4 months, teachers were surveyed about the peer social integration of their student, researchers observed student‐peer interactions and students reported on their social satisfaction. Teacher reports of student social integration were positively correlated with observers' positive peer social interaction scores. However, child‐reported loneliness was not correlated with either teacher‐reported social integration or observer ratings of peer interactions. Autistic children consistently reported less loneliness than teacher and researcher observations of their socializing might suggest. title: Transforming south African special schools for autism inclusion: Strengthening teachers' knowledge and practices
text_snippet: Transforming south African special schools for autism inclusion: Strengthening teachers' knowledge and practices Abstract Implementation of inclusive education in South Africa faces significant challenges, particularly in supporting learners with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). A key issue is the lack of teachers' preparedness to create autism‐inclusive learning environments. This challenge remains insufficiently addressed, particularly in under‐resourced contexts and limits teachers' ability to practise inclusive education. Guided by Variation Theory, this study utilised qualitative research approach and phenomenological case study design to gain participants' in‐depth understanding of ASD and how these influence their pedagogical practices in special schools. The research design was employed in four special schools in the King Cetshwayo District. Data were generated through semi‐structured interviews and analysed using a thematic approach. The findings indicate that teachers employ adaptive strategies such as differentiated instruction, visual support, concrete materials, concise instructions, and structured routines for inclusion of learners with ASD. title: When coping is not inclusion: Practitioner assessment narratives and the sustainability of autistic participation in mainstream schools
text_snippet: When coping is not inclusion: Practitioner assessment narratives and the sustainability of autistic participation in mainstream schools Abstract Inclusive education is often evaluated through visible indicators such as classroom engagement, behaviour, attendance and academic participation. For autistic learners, however, visible functioning may not fully reflect the accessibility of the educational environment or the regulatory effort required to sustain participation. This paper examines a purposively selected set of cases in which autistic learners were described as coping or participating in mainstream education while assessment documentation also recorded evidence of strain, environmental dependence or difficulty sustaining participation across contexts and time. Drawing on qualitative analysis of nine anonymised practitioner assessment narratives integrating school and family perspectives, the study explores how participation was represented within real‐world assessment documentation. Reflexive thematic analysis identified recurring patterns in which participation depended on environmental structuring, behavioural adaptation, adult mediation and sustained self‐regulation. title: ‘I'm still guessing what's happening and what I'm meant to do’: Special educator experiences of supporting echolalic students
text_snippet: ‘I'm still guessing what's happening and what I'm meant to do’: Special educator experiences of supporting echolalic students Abstract Echolalia has been widely examined in clinical and developmental research, yet the experiences of teachers, who arguably encounter echolalia across the widest variety of contexts and environments, remain largely unexplored. This study examined special education teachers lived experiences of echolalia in specialist schools. Using a qualitative design, semi‐structured interviews were conducted with 83 special education teachers. Data was analysed using qualitative thematic analysis. Five interconnected practice problems emerged: limited foundational knowledge, lack of classroom‐based strategies, inconsistent speech pathology interpretations, limited specialist presence and unclear professional roles. This study found that teachers' experiences of echolalia are not only shaped by echoes themselves, but also by the fragmented knowledge, structural constraints and ambiguous professional responsibility within special education systems.

title: A call‐out for AAC professional development training: Special education teachers speak‐up
text_snippet: A call‐out for AAC professional development training: Special education teachers speak‐up Abstract Evidence suggests that special education teachers are not well‐prepared to implement services for students who may benefit from augmentative and alternative communication. The lack of training often emerges during their pre‐service teacher preparation programs. To alleviate the knowledge gap, special education teachers may rely on professional development training opportunities. As a result, to better understand the perspectives of special education teachers on the state of AAC professional development training an online survey was conducted across the United States. A total of 772 special education teachers provided their views through five identified themes. These included that AAC professional development ‘training is available,’ there is a ‘need for training,’ there are ‘systemic barriers’ to training, ‘team support’ was used as a means for training, and participants were ‘unclear or did not know’ if AAC professional development training was available. Results suggested that most participants indicated that AAC professional development training is lacking, and that training is needed. title: Ethical challenges in the inclusion of pupils with special needs in mainstream schools: A social ecological model perspective
text_snippet: Ethical challenges in the inclusion of pupils with special needs in mainstream schools: A social ecological model perspective Abstract The inclusion of pupils with special needs in mainstream schools presents complex ethical dilemmas for educational staff, school leaders and families. This research explores these dilemmas through Bronfenbrenner's social ecological model in the context of Israel's 2018 inclusion reform, highlighting the interaction between schoolchildren and their environment across five subsystems. Semi‐structured interviews were conducted with 83 educators holding diverse school roles across Israel. Using grounded theory analysis, findings demonstrated that although ethical dilemmas appeared across all ecological systems, they were concentrated within the exosystem where organisational structures, resource limitations and policy implementation conditions constrained educators’ ability to enact inclusive practices. Two dominant categories of ethical dilemmas were identified: balancing inclusive participation with effective classroom functioning, and managing tensions between parental preferences and professional educational judgement. title: Inclusion matters: Learning in collaboration with students with profound intellectual and multiple disabilities
text_snippet: Inclusion matters: Learning in collaboration with students with profound intellectual and multiple disabilities Abstract Children with profound intellectual and multiple disabilities are rarely included in discussions of inclusion/inclusive education. This paper begins from the premise that their inclusion matters and that it is helpful to begin at the level of the classroom where children and teachers have some agency. The aim is to make students with profound intellectual and multiple disabilities the focus of discussion of inclusion and belonging, and to show how, by seeking to research their lived experience with them, we can shed light on matters that are important. The work draws on theory concerning relational belonging encompassing affect, attachment, people, places and temporal rhythms, plus occupational science theory about co‐occupation characterised by shared physicality, intentionality and emotionality. From case study research conducted in a special school in England, the vignette method used stresses embodied attentiveness and knowing. The findings show the physical, embodied, time and place, and co‐occupation dimensions associated with achieving belonging in a special school classroom that are likely to matter to broader inclusive education. title: Perspectives of the COVID ‐19 pandemic: Views of young people with special educational needs and/or disabilities
text_snippet: Perspectives of the COVID ‐19 pandemic: Views of young people with special educational needs and/or disabilities Abstract This qualitative study directly engaged 46 young people (YP) with Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND), aged 14–25, who were in education, to discover their experiences during the COVID‐19 pandemic (2020–2022). Unlike past research relying on parents or professionals, this study captured their voices directly regarding daily life, education, and relationships. The disruption of the pandemic severely impacted education, wellbeing, and connection with family and peers. Additionally, online learning proved unsuitable due to specific SEND barriers and course requirements. Overall, most individuals found the period challenging, though a small minority welcomed the changes. The majority showed resilience over time but would not want to experience it again.

title: Decoloniality, staff development and the limits of inclusive education in UK higher education: A reflexive case study
text_snippet: Decoloniality, staff development and the limits of inclusive education in UK higher education: A reflexive case study Abstract Inclusive education in higher education is increasingly framed through commitments to equity, diversity, and epistemic justice, yet the enactment of these commitments remains uneven and contested. This qualitative case study examines a cross‐disciplinary staff development initiative at a UK post‐92 university that engaged academic and professional services staff with decolonial approaches to curriculum design. Grounded conceptually in praxis, positionality and pluriversality, the initiative comprised participatory workshops and a practical toolkit intended to support critical reflection on colonial legacies in teaching and learning. Data were generated through workshop feedback, reflective testimonies and follow‐up consultations with 40 self‐selecting participants across education, health, business and professional services. Reflexive thematic analysis indicates that the initiative functioned primarily as a space for conceptual clarification and affective engagement rather than sustained pedagogical or structural transformation. title: Considerations from a pilot study: Informing future research on gender and sexuality diverse autistic students' perspectives of Internet threats
text_snippet: Considerations from a pilot study: Informing future research on gender and sexuality diverse autistic students' perspectives of Internet threats Abstract Autistic students often face unique challenges related to Internet threats. When intersected with gender and sexuality diversity, challenges can compound and lead to increased risk of bullying, discrimination, marginalisation and exclusion. Although there is an intersection between autism and gender and sexuality diversity, the voices of gender and sexuality diverse autistic students about Internet threats remain an underexplored research area. Most studies have focused on neurotypical, heterosexual and cis‐gender students or addressed autism, sexuality and gender separately. This paper builds on findings from a recent exploratory pilot study offering new empirical insight into autistic perceived Internet threats—an area currently underrepresented in inclusive education and digital safety. This paper presents considerations from the exploratory pilot study to inform future research on gender and sexuality diverse autistic students' perspectives on Internet threats. title: Inclusive education in Portugal: 50 years following the 25th April revolution
text_snippet: Inclusive education in Portugal: 50 years following the 25th April revolution Abstract After the 25th of April 1974, Portugal was marked by legislative developments in major areas defining a democratic society, including education. The aim of this paper is to describe a comprehensive analysis of the legislation on education for children with disabilities in Portugal, exploring commonalities with international developments regarding children's rights and access to education. A document analysis was conducted on the chronology of laws on education for children with disabilities over the last 50 years coupled with assessment of quantitative indicators of their access to mainstream schools. Findings confirm the accomplishment of significant legislative developments following the 25th April 1974 affirming and reaffirming the right of children with disabilities to education in mainstream settings and establishing support for them to succeed in school. Legislative developments were analysed within Göransson & Nilholm's framework (2014), describing evolving categories to education from physical placement in mainstream schools towards the building of an inclusive and supportive school community based on principles of equity, care and justice. title: A multidimensional learning outcomes instrument for students with special educational needs: Evidence from content validity index analysis
text_snippet: A multidimensional learning outcomes instrument for students with special educational needs: Evidence from content validity index analysis Abstract Valid assessment in special and inclusive education requires instruments capable of capturing the multidimensional learning outcomes of students with Special Educational Needs (SEN). This study examined the content validity of a newly developed, teacher‐rated SEN outcomes instrument grounded in Bloom's Taxonomy, which assesses cognitive, affective, and psychomotor development in school settings. Using the Content Validity Index (CVI) approach, eight experts in educational management, special education and educational assessment evaluated 19 items on a four‐point relevance scale. Item‐level (I‐CVI) and scale‐level (S‐CVI/Ave and S‐CVI/UA) indices were computed following established guidelines. Seventeen items achieved full agreement (I‐CVI = 1.00), one met the acceptable threshold (I‐CVI = 0.88) and one was removed for insufficient relevance (I‐CVI = 0.75). Initial values (S‐CVI/Ave = 0.98, S‐CVI/UA = 0.89) exceeded recommended standards. After the item was removed, the final 18‐item instrument reached S‐CVI/Ave = 0.99 and S‐CVI/UA = 0.94, indicating excellent content validity. title: “I think people's perception that her reading is good enough. That would be a worry to me.” Mother and child perspectives of school‐related reading for children with Down syndrome
text_snippet: “I think people's perception that her reading is good enough. That would be a worry to me.” Mother and child perspectives of school‐related reading for children with Down syndrome Abstract There is growing interest in children's reading experiences, both volitional and those initiated by, or connected to, school‐related reading. However, the majority of this research focuses on the reading experiences of neurotypical children; limiting understanding and the potential to improve support for other groups of children. This study examined the school‐related reading experiences of children with Down syndrome, through semi‐structured interviews with 10 mothers and 9 children (aged 5–13, mean age 10) from the UK. Utilising an inductive approach to thematic analysis, school factors (staff and provision) were reported by mothers to be essential to support their child's reading, with specialist training, knowledge of their child, personalised reading instruction/support and high aspirations all important. Parents also discussed: the blending of mainstream (e.g. phonics) and specialist (e.g. specific reading scheme) reading instructional approaches and resources; reading within a broader picture of their child's development; and the importance of home‐school connections to support their child's reading. title: Exploring factors influencing self‐advocacy in students with learning disabilities: A qualitative study
text_snippet: Exploring factors influencing self‐advocacy in students with learning disabilities: A qualitative study Abstract Self‐advocacy is a central component of educational inclusion for students with learning disabilities because it enables students to recognize their learning needs, communicate those needs, request accommodations and participate more actively in decisions affecting their education. However, students often develop self‐advocacy within emotionally demanding and institutionally inconsistent contexts. This study aimed to explore the lived experiences of students with learning disabilities and identify the internal, relational and institutional factors that shape their self‐advocacy in secondary and post‐secondary educational settings. A qualitative descriptive‐interpretive design was used. Semi‐structured interviews were conducted with 26 students aged 14–22 years in Richmond Hill, Canada, all of whom had a formal learning disability diagnosis. Participants were recruited from secondary and post‐secondary educational settings and support networks. Interviews were audio‐recorded, transcribed verbatim and analysed in NVivo‐15 using open, axial and selective coding. title: Differentiation‐related tensions in the thinking and instruction of Eritrean elementary and middle school mathematics teachers
text_snippet: Differentiation‐related tensions in the thinking and instruction of Eritrean elementary and middle school mathematics teachers Abstract Differentiated instruction is key to implementing inclusive education and addressing the individual needs of all students. This study explores the pedagogical tensions related to differentiation in Eritrean elementary and middle school mathematics teachers' thinking and instruction practices. The research data consist of 8 teacher interviews and video recordings of their teaching in 10 mathematics lessons. The findings from a thematic analysis reveal three tensions: adapting instruction to students' individual needs versus carrying out whole‐class frontal teaching; providing individual tasks versus abstract content‐laden teaching; and utilising peer learning versus emphasising individual‐oriented competition. The study highlights the need to increase Eritrean mathematics teachers' awareness of the contradictory discourses surrounding classroom practices. Teachers require both material and professional support and training on research‐based differentiated instruction practices to foster the inclusion of all students.

title: Designing for inclusion through online professional learning: A content analysis of teachers' reasonable adjustments
text_snippet: Designing for inclusion through online professional learning: A content analysis of teachers' reasonable adjustments Abstract Reasonable adjustments are changes or accommodations to instruction, curriculum and assessment that allow students with disability to access and participate in education on the same basis as peers without disability. The aim of this study was to examine how professional learning can strengthen teachers' capability to design inclusive reasonable adjustments aligned with the Social Model of Disability and Multi‐Tiered Systems of Support. This study draws on data collected as part of a randomised controlled trial that assessed the effectiveness of an online professional learning intervention on reasonable adjustments for educational stakeholders in mainstream primary school settings. Using content analysis, we examined the characteristics of adjustments suggested by teaching staff ( n = 10) and analysed differences between intervention and control group participants, and before and after intervention. Findings indicated a shift among intervention participants from individualised towards whole‐classroom adjustments designed to benefit all students. title: Resource centres as a support measure for inclusion: The voices of special education professionals
text_snippet: Resource centres as a support measure for inclusion: The voices of special education professionals Abstract The right to education for all students is difficult to reconcile with the persistence of segregated schooling modalities. Thus, special schools can no longer be justified as separate settings for certain students. In Spain, a reform process is under way that reorients these institutions as support structures for mainstream schools. This article examines how special school professionals understand and evaluate the resource‐centre role performed by their institutions and its perceived contribution to inclusive education. A qualitative study was conducted with 142 professionals, all employed by the 13 special schools in the Region of Murcia (Spain). Data were collected through semi‐structured interviews and analysed inductively using ATLAS.ti. Participants perceive the main strengths of this role to be specialized guidance, training and advisory support; digital and material resources; and its perceived contribution to collaboration and inclusive practices. title: An investigation into the key factors for implementing total quality management within an Irish national agency supporting special education
text_snippet: An investigation into the key factors for implementing total quality management within an Irish national agency supporting special education Abstract This study is conducted within the Irish National Council for Special Education (NCSE). After a decade of extensive change in special education, the Irish Government is enabling the NCSE to undertake substantial reform. Total Quality Management (TQM), a strategic means of improving provision, has been introduced to enhance special education support for students, families and schools. This study investigated the key factors for implementing TQM within the NCSE. Qualitative methods, in the form of semi‐structured interviews with the NCSE TQM steering committee, were applied to explore literature review informed education TQM factors. Interpretive Structural Modelling (ISM) was used to generate a TQM key factor implementation framework for the NCSE. 10 key factors of leadership commitment, staff ownership, customer focus, stakeholder engagement, strategic planning, professional development, communication, process management, management information systems and continuous improvement were identified for implementing TQM within the NCSE. A key factor implementation framework was produced. This study presents a suggested framework for TQM within special education support agencies

title: Measuring what matters: Operationalizing neurodiversity‐affirming practices through participatory design of STEM workshops for autistic youth
text_snippet: Measuring what matters: Operationalizing neurodiversity‐affirming practices through participatory design of STEM workshops for autistic youth Abstract Limited research has examined how neurodiversity‐affirming approaches are (1) co‐created with autistic people, (2) operationalized, (3) implemented, (4) assessed and (5) iterated. Across a 3‐year program of research, we co‐developed and iterated game design and employment workshops for and with autistic youth. After encountering difficulties enacting authentically neurodiversity‐affirming approaches during the Year 2 workshop, we developed neurodiversity‐affirming principles that guided hiring, training, curriculum development and student and staff advocacy opportunities in Year 3 workshops. We assessed fidelity to these principles. This paper examines if these changes were associated with increases in: 1) neurodiversity‐affirming staff practices and (2) student engagement with workshop content. Masked coders analysed the following data sources from Years 2 and 3: (1) video recordings of staff teaching practices, (2) pre‐ and post‐workshop staff surveys and (3) students' ratings of engagement with workshop activities. title: Pilot study of a brief inclusive peer intervention in middle school: Staff and student perspectives on inclusion
text_snippet: Pilot study of a brief inclusive peer intervention in middle school: Staff and student perspectives on inclusion Abstract Peer relationships are essential to well‐being, yet children with disabilities are frequently isolated within school settings. This pilot study explored students with neurodevelopmental disabilities (NDDs), peers, and educators' experiences with a brief peer‐focused intervention in a middle school, and its effects on peer attitudes towards students with NDDs. The intervention incorporated (1) education to peers about disability and strategies to engage with children with NDDs, and (2) facilitated opportunities for social interactions between peers and children with NDDs through activity‐based recess clubs. A mixed‐methods, convergent parallel design was used. Peer attitudes towards children with disabilities were measured using the CATCH‐Revised Questionnaire pre and post the educational session. Interviews with children with disabilities ( n = 2), peers ( n = 8), and teachers ( n = 2) explored perceptions of the intervention on inclusion. title: Inclusionary leadership and professional learning: Communities of practice as catalysts for inclusive schooling in autism education
text_snippet: Inclusionary leadership and professional learning: Communities of practice as catalysts for inclusive schooling in autism education Abstract The expansion of autism special classes in mainstream schools has reshaped the demands on principals' leadership and professional learning. This study examines how primary school principals in Ireland enact inclusionary leadership within autism special class contexts with a particular focus on professional learning and collaborative practice. The research uses an interpretive qualitative design, based on semi‐structured interviews with fifteen primary school principals responsible for autism special classes. Data were analysed with thematic analysis to explore how principals supported staff learning and inclusive practice. The findings demonstrate that inconsistent preparation pathways for teachers and principals require leaders to actively facilitate professional learning within the school context. Principals supported staff development through mentoring, reflective dialogue and collaborative problem‐solving, often embedding professional learning within everyday practice. title: A level playing field: PLCs as a sustainable model of professional learning to support the enactment of inclusive pedagogy to support all learners in post‐primary schools
text_snippet: A level playing field: PLCs as a sustainable model of professional learning to support the enactment of inclusive pedagogy to support all learners in post‐primary schools Abstract Despite the strong policy and legislative context for inclusive education worldwide, its definition lacks consensus, and debate exists around its enactment. While there is growing research on how inclusive pedagogy can support teachers to create inclusive classrooms, it mainly relates to primary education. Given the distinct challenges to inclusion in post‐primary schools, research explicitly focusing on how to enact inclusive pedagogy in these settings is essential. This is particularly important in the Republic of Ireland in the context of increasing diversity of learning needs and the significant need for teacher professional learning (PL) in this area. This study aims to address gaps in the literature by exploring how professional learning communities (PLCs) in two Irish post‐primary schools supported teacher enactment of inclusive pedagogy to meet the needs of all learners through a school‐university partnership. Qualitative data from 20 participants revealed that the PLCs were an effective structure for collaboration that supported teachers to enact inclusive pedagogy. title: Touch, sound and memory in inclusive art education: Participatory clay‐and‐sound workshops with visually impaired students
text_snippet: Touch, sound and memory in inclusive art education: Participatory clay‐and‐sound workshops with visually impaired students Abstract In Indonesia, visual arts education for students with visual impairments remains limited, although contemporary art practices involving touch, sound and material exploration may offer alternatives to visually oriented forms of representation. This study examined how clay‐and‐sound workshops could be adapted for visually impaired students and how different visual profiles shaped engagement with sound, memory and tactile making. Five students aged 16–20 participated in a five‐week workshop at SLBN A Citeureup, Indonesia: two with blindness, two with low vision and one with multiple disabilities and visual impairment. Students listened to nature soundscapes and translated sensory, emotional and mnemonic responses into non‐representational clay forms. Data included field notes, interviews, visual and audiovisual documentation and reflective journals. Three patterns of tactile engagement emerged. Students with blindness showed immediate sound‐to‐material responses; students with low vision used deliberate sensory‐focusing strategies, including closing their eyes; and the student with multiple disabilities engaged through repeated forms and verbal narration. journal_name: Journal of Research in Special Educational Needs
title: Did mathematics achievement gaps for students with disabilities widen after the introduction of the Common Core and its aligned assessments?
text_snippet: Did mathematics achievement gaps for students with disabilities widen after the introduction of the Common Core and its aligned assessments? Abstract This study addresses the important yet underexplored question of whether the Common Core State Standards in Mathematics, first introduced in the United States in 2009 and which emphasize critical thinking and problem‐solving, as well as the computer‐based assessments aligned with the Common Core, have facilitated or hindered learning for students with disabilities. By analysing administrative data from a large county in California, we track mathematics achievement trends before and after the implementation of the Common Core. Our findings show a significant widening of the achievement disparity in mathematics between students with and without disabilities, suggesting that the Common Core and computerized assessments may have disproportionately affected students with disabilities.

title: When educational pathways become fragile: Teachers' perspectives on the schooling of autistic students
text_snippet: When educational pathways become fragile: Teachers' perspectives on the schooling of autistic students Abstract International research indicates elevated levels of educational instability among autistic students, including school mobility and exclusion. However, systematic evidence on how such trajectories are experienced within differentiated education systems remains limited, particularly from teachers' perspectives in Germany. The present study examines teacher‐reported educational pathways of autistic students across school types, focusing on patterns of instability, institutional conditions and professional challenges. A total of N = 392 teachers completed an anonymous online survey. Data were analysed using a two‐stage strategy combining descriptive analyses with exploratory inferential analyses within a defined subsample. Teachers predominantly described educational trajectories as fluctuating and recurrently challenging, whereas formal exclusionary events were reported as rare or limited to individual cases. This pattern indicates that instability may not primarily manifest in formally recorded events but rather in ongoing challenges within everyday school participation. title: Perspectives of autistic students on school leadership practices supporting their well‐being in mainstream schools
text_snippet: Perspectives of autistic students on school leadership practices supporting their well‐being in mainstream schools Abstract Autistic students in mainstream schools often need additional support to feel included and experience a sense of well‐being. While school leaders play a key role in fostering inclusive environments, research on the views of autistic students about these leaders' roles, particularly principals, remains limited. This article addresses this gap, presenting findings from a photovoice study with autistic adolescents (aged 12–15) about their sense of safety and well‐being in mainstream schools in Victoria, Australia, with findings on school leadership drawn from three participants' accounts. Data analysis, conducted through a constructivist grounded theory approach, suggested that school leaders who engaged, listened, allocated resources, and facilitated school‐level transitions were perceived as contributing positively to participants' comfort and inclusion. The findings highlight the importance of inclusive leadership in supporting autistic students. Future studies should incorporate student voices in exploring leadership practices and examine the broader role of school leaders in promoting well‐being and inclusion.

title: Job satisfaction and occupational burnout in special education personnel: Meta‐analysis
text_snippet: Job satisfaction and occupational burnout in special education personnel: Meta‐analysis Abstract This meta‐analysis examined the relationship between job satisfaction and occupational burnout among special education personnel, including special education teachers and related professionals working in special education settings. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a comprehensive search was conducted across Google Scholar, ERIC, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Dergipark and the YÖK Thesis Database. Eighteen quantitative studies ( k = 18), published between 2014 and 2025, met the inclusion criteria. Only studies reporting Pearson correlation coefficients were included. Effect sizes were calculated using R software with the metafor package, and a random‐effects model was applied. Results revealed a moderate and statistically significant negative association between job satisfaction and burnout ( r = −0.344, p I 2 = 97.39%), suggesting substantial variability across studies. Publication bias analyses indicated no significant asymmetry. These findings underscore the importance of organizational and psychological interventions aimed at improving working conditions and supporting the well‐being of special education personnel. title: An empirical investigation of contextual barriers and academic achievement disparities for students with disabilities in South Gondar primary schools, Ethiopia
text_snippet: An empirical investigation of contextual barriers and academic achievement disparities for students with disabilities in South Gondar primary schools, Ethiopia Abstract This study assessed contextual barriers and academic achievement disparities for students with disabilities (SWDs) in South Gondar Primary Schools, Ethiopia. A convergent parallel mixed‐methods design with an ex post facto quantitative component was employed. A sample of 544 participants (227 SWDs, 317 students without disabilities) was selected from five primary schools. Quantitative data from continuous assessment scores were analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics. Qualitative data from semi‐structured interviews and focus group discussions were analysed thematically. A statistically significant academic achievement disparity was found between SWDs (M = 33.22, SD = 34.44) and their peers (M = 70.55, SD = 12.53), t (542) = −12.02, p F (4, 222) = 6.24, p η 2 = 0.10. Key barriers reported included a severe shortage of special needs teachers, inaccessible physical infrastructure, lack of teaching materials and assistive technology and pervasive negative attitudes. The large academic achievement gap is strongly associated with systemic and attitudinal barriers rather than individual incapability. title: Mainstream teachers, collegial learning and inclusive education in Sweden
text_snippet: Mainstream teachers, collegial learning and inclusive education in Sweden Abstract While educational inclusion is national policy in many countries, good practice is slow to emerge. The study investigated mainstream teachers' orientation towards collegial learning while they participated in a national professionalization programme aimed at expanding schools' capacity for inclusive education in Sweden. Qualitative data collected from a total of 30 interviews and 60 observations from 30 schools who participated in the national professionalization programme were re‐analysed. Results suggest that teachers are both willing and feel able to strive for more inclusive education through collegial learning. However, the data also suggest that vague goals undermine effective use of collegial learning in schools and that national (or above school‐level) coordination of collegial learning practice is needed to achieve goals that are located beyond teachers' and their school's most immediate needs.

title: Rural views on community and the inclusion of students with disabilities: “They’re Community Members”
text_snippet: Rural views on community and the inclusion of students with disabilities: “They’re Community Members” Abstract This study addressed the use of inclusive educational practices in two districts nominated by scholars of inclusive education across the USA. The two districts that eventually agreed to be studied were located in rural places. This article analyzes and interprets study data to address the local features related to inclusive educational practice in these places in order to derive insights that might benefit districts elsewhere, including in both rural and more urbanized locales. The key conclusion highlights the importance of community in securing and sustaining local support—such a connection builds a mutually constitutive relationship that propagates understanding of and support for inclusive practices. This study expands on our earlier work, which revealed several promising strategies that districts might use when adopting inclusive practices, including maintaining an identity of inclusivity and using community‐grounded and systemic approaches. It seems that sustainable inclusive practice benefits from, or perhaps requires, community understanding and support. title: ‘Because if you get it right at that level, then you’re getting it right for everybody’: Teacher perspectives on facilitating the transition to primary school for children with additional support needs
text_snippet: ‘Because if you get it right at that level, then you’re getting it right for everybody’: Teacher perspectives on facilitating the transition to primary school for children with additional support needs Abstract The transition to primary school is typically more challenging for children with additional support needs (ASN). This is notable, as a positive experience at the transition to school is associated with greater wellbeing, school engagement, and academic outcomes. Practices and support for this transition are common and varied; however, the extent to which practices are appropriate or modified to support children with ASN to flourish during their first years of schooling is unclear. The UK government's recent aim to improve early school outcomes in England will necessitate an understanding of how to adequately support children with ASN at this transition. In this exploratory study, we interviewed seven teachers in England and Scotland about their experiences of supporting children with ASN at the transition to primary school. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we developed four themes: good intentions but lack of evidence for effective practice; differentiated practice is good, but changing the whole system would be better; neither country gets it quite right; and need to look beyond the initial transition. title: Inclusive cycle training: Using the COM ‐B model to examine the attitudes, perceptions and behaviours of cycle instructors
text_snippet: Inclusive cycle training: Using the COM ‐B model to examine the attitudes, perceptions and behaviours of cycle instructors Abstract This is the first study to comprehensively consider cycle instructor knowledge, motivation and behaviour when teaching children with disabilities. Using a prospective design, we used a questionnaire to measure COM‐B components before ( N = 845), immediately after ( N = 480) and 6 months after ( N = 63) an online course for instructors. We also conducted interviews ( N = 12) 3 months after training. Prior to the course, physical opportunity and psychological capability were the biggest barriers to delivering inclusive cycle training. In addition, motivation was important in predicting adaptations to training. Scores on all factors increased immediately following the course, 6 months later only an increase in psychological capability was maintained. Qualitative data highlighted behavioural changes as a consequence of the course, which were captured in the quantitative data. 6 months after the course social opportunity was an important predictor of behaviour, highlighting the importance of social influence and support. title: Accelerating equity: The causal impact of syntactic bootstrapping on inclusive education and SDG 4 for autistic children
text_snippet: Accelerating equity: The causal impact of syntactic bootstrapping on inclusive education and SDG 4 for autistic children Abstract To address critical challenges in inclusive education for autistic children under Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4), this study examined the causal impact of a syntactic bootstrapping intervention on language development and classroom participation. title: Collaborative action research for inclusive teacher professional learning in early childhood education
text_snippet: Collaborative action research for inclusive teacher professional learning in early childhood education Abstract Inclusive Early Childhood Development and Education (ECDE) requires teachers with the knowledge, skills, and professional agency to respond effectively to diverse classrooms. Despite policy commitments to inclusive education across Africa, many ECDE teachers experience inadequate preparation, fragmented professional development, and limited institutional support. Collaborative participatory action research (PAR) offers a promising approach to teacher professional learning, yet evidence from African contexts remains limited. This study examined how collaborative PAR influenced inclusive teaching competencies among ECDE teachers participating in a regional professional learning initiative across six countries in Southern and Eastern Africa. A qualitative PAR design involved 35 purposively selected teachers over 12 months. Data from project reports, reflective journals, and focus group discussions were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. title: Utilising collaborative practice to sustain teacher resilience
text_snippet: Utilising collaborative practice to sustain teacher resilience Abstract Teacher resilience is an often overlooked and under‐researched area in the Irish context. Research on teacher resilience is presented as the ability to sustain wellbeing and to respond adaptively and resiliently to professional challenges in the face of ‘unavoidable uncertainties’ (The signature pedagogies of the profession of law, medicine, engineering and the clergy, 2005, p. 1) inherent in the realities of teaching (Asia‐Pacific Journal of Teacher Education, 24, 2013, p. 288). Previous work in this area concentrated primarily on initial teacher education and early career teachers. This mixed‐methods multi‐site case study examined the resilience of 137 teachers and school leaders at primary level from 2016 to 2021 in response to systemic changes. A central focus was on the lived experience of participants and their career‐wide resiliency. Survey and interview data were collected during the final school term of the 2020/21 school year which was a particularly challenging time for schools during the Covid‐19 pandemic.
